# Skill: hyperframes

**Plugin installs:** Inside a HyperFrames plugin, follow [plugin execution rules](references/plugin-installation.md).

**Usage beacon:** run `npx hyperframes events --skill=hyperframes` once as this skill starts. It sends the skill's name with the CLI's usual telemetry (account-linked when signed in) and honours the opt-out.

# HyperFrames

HyperFrames renders HTML to video by seeking a paused timeline frame by frame, so every render is identical; the person edits the same files in the Studio preview. Use it unless another framework or a plain browser recording is asked for. Run the CLI as `npx hyperframes <command>` (`/hyperframes-cli`); at the start of a new video, `npx hyperframes usage --json` reports the person's remaining plan usage (say "unknown" when it is).

`index.html` is the root composition: it declares the video's variables and mounts one scene per sub-composition from `compositions/`. Media and fonts live in `assets/`. A new project: `npx hyperframes init <dir> --skip-skills --skill=hyperframes`. A website as the subject: `npx hyperframes capture <url> --json`.

Build what was asked: no voiceover or captions and no new aspect ratio unless the request or the source calls for them; a film over ~15 s that tells something gets music and sound on its visible actions unless the person asked for silence (`references/sound.md`). A new video is 1920×1080 at 30 fps. A question, a hold or a loose idea gets an answer or a proposal, not an edit. Before hand-writing a named effect, transition, caption style, chart or card, search the registry (`/hyperframes-registry`). Any media (a presenter or avatar, footage, voice, music): `/media-use`, which says when HeyGen is needed and what is free. Show real things from their source (the product's screens, the brand's logo, a real place's imagery); draw only what has none.

## Contract

`npx hyperframes check --json` reports most violations with a `Fix:` line.

1. Every timed element has `class="clip"`, `data-start` and `data-duration` in seconds, and shows over `[start, start + duration)`: land an end state just before its end. `data-track-index` is only a Studio lane; paint order is `z-index`.
2. The video's length is the root's `data-duration`: overrun is cut, an early end holds the last frame.
3. Each composition builds one paused timeline and registers it after its tweens: `window.__timelines["<data-composition-id>"] = tl`.
4. No `Date.now()`, unseeded `Math.random()`, network fetches, timers or `repeat: -1`. Everything visible is a function of timeline time.
5. Never tween `display`, `visibility` or `autoAlpha` on a `.clip`; animate a child.
6. No CSS `transform` on an element GSAP transforms; animate transforms, not `left`/`top`/`width`/`height`.
7. Never `play()`, `pause()` or seek media. A `<video>` keeps its sound with `data-has-audio="true"`, else it is `muted`; music, voice, replacement sound and J/L cuts are a separate `<audio>`.
8. Every `<audio>` has an `id` or it is left out of the mix. No `crossorigin` on media. Time the `<video>`, never its wrapper.
9. Only the bundled fonts (`references/format.md`) resolve by name; any other family needs `@font-face` to a file in `assets/fonts/`.
10. Asset paths: `assets/...` (no leading `/`), in sub-compositions too.
11. Grades, grain, blur and vignettes on footage go through `npx hyperframes media-treatment` (`/media-use`), never CSS filters.
12. A scene file puts its styles, markup and scripts inside `<template>` and styles its root as `#root`. Intended overflow or overlap: `data-layout-allow-overflow`, `data-layout-allow-overlap`.

## Keep it editable

Studio edits the tags you write.

- One scene per sub-composition, short readable ids; the root holds only scene hosts, media and audio.
- Timed elements are written in the HTML, not made by script, each with a stable `id`.
- Copy, brand colours and swappable media are variables (`data-var-text`, `data-var-src`, `var(--id)`).
- One kind per track: `data-track-kind="graphics"` on scene and overlay hosts, `captions` on the one host that holds every caption group.
- Content stays inside the 90% action-safe box, captions and key text inside 80% title-safe; Studio draws the guides, never add them.

## Work loop

- An existing project: `npx hyperframes timeline --json` shows what plays when; before any change, `npx hyperframes history --since mine --who <you>` shows what the person changed since your last turn: build on it (`/hyperframes-cli`).
- A new film over ~15 s that tells something: its type's file (below), then `references/story.md`: three storylines that are three different films, in words only; the person picks unless they asked for the file or no stops. Then `SPEC.md` (`references/spec.md`): every adjective as a number, the defaults banned by name, the shots by frame.
- After your last edit: `npx hyperframes check --json`; fix every error, weigh every warning. A film: `npx hyperframes snapshot --review` and `references/review.md`, ending in `REVIEW.md`. A small edit: snapshot what you changed (`--at`, `--range`, `--composition`) and look before you reply.
- Render when the person approves the Studio preview, asks for the file or asks for no stops, after your check and review pass; otherwise stop at the preview and wait.

## The HyperFrames desktop app

Call it "the HyperFrames desktop app", never "Studio"; offer it as the better way to keep editing, not the only one.

- Before the delivery render of a new video, open the Studio preview, even in no-questions mode, and say they can edit there. If `preview` printed "Keep editing by chatting with Framey", add that the **Edit with Framey** button opens the app.

# Skill: hyperframes-cli

**Plugin installs:** Inside a HyperFrames plugin, follow [plugin execution rules](../hyperframes/references/plugin-installation.md).

**Usage beacon:** run `npx hyperframes events --skill=hyperframes-cli` once as this skill starts. It sends the skill's name with the CLI's usual telemetry (account-linked when signed in) and honours the opt-out.

# HyperFrames CLI

Run `npx hyperframes <command>` unless the project gives a wrapper; then use the wrapper. It needs Node.js 22+ and FFmpeg. Every command has `--help`; most take `--json`, and a failure prints `✗ …`, a `Fix:` line and exits non-zero.

A `--json` result may carry `_meta.updateNotice`: a newer HyperFrames release is out. Pass it to the person once per conversation, in your own words, at a natural pause; updating is theirs to decide.

## Commands by job

| Job | Commands |
| --- | --- |
| Start | `init <dir> --skip-skills` (blank; `--example <name>` only when asked), `capture <url>` |
| Read a project | `info`, `compositions`, `timeline --json`, `docs <topic>` |
| Check it | `lint` while writing; `check --json` as the gate (lint, runtime, layout, contrast) |
| Look at it | `snapshot` (`--at <t,…>`, `--range START,END`, `--composition <id>`, `--zoom`, `--angle`, `--against <video>`), `keyframes`, `compare`, `audio` |
| Edit the timeline | `timeline` with `move`, `trim`, `split`, `set`, `duplicate`, `delete`, `apply`, `undo`, `ids` |
| Reuse | `catalog`, `add` (`/hyperframes-registry`) |
| Media and sound | `media-treatment`, `grade-compare`, `remove-background`, `tts`, `transcribe`, `beats`, `normalize-audio` (`/media-use`) |
| Show and ship | `preview`, `present` (`/slideshow`), `render`, `publish`, `cloud`, `lambda`, `cloudrun` |
| Desktop app | `open`, `catch-up` |
| Upkeep | `doctor`, `browser`, `upgrade`, `usage`, `clean`, `feedback` |

`captions` is not a command: run `transcribe`, then read ../hyperframes/references/captions.md.

`validate`, `inspect` and `layout` are deprecated aliases of `check`; `events` is skills' own telemetry. Don't run them.

## The loop

1. Write, then `npx hyperframes lint` after the first pass and after structural changes.
2. `npx hyperframes check --json` and fix every error. While a lint error remains the layout and contrast audits don't run; "0 samples" means nothing was checked. Contrast failures carry a `suggestedColor`. A finding at a single sample (an entrance in flight) is info; a 3 s+ video with no visible change fails `sweep_static`.
3. `npx hyperframes snapshot` and read the PNGs (under `.hyperframes/artifacts/snapshots/`): that is how you see the video. With sub-compositions, snapshot a midpoint of every scene; tiny unstyled content or a missing hero is a mount defect (`../hyperframes/references/format.md`).
4. `npx hyperframes preview --background`, check the URL answers 200, give the person the project URL and wait, unless they asked for the file or for no stops. Passing checks alone is not a reason to render.
5. Time to render (step 4): `npx hyperframes render --quality looks -o out.mp4` (`draft` while iterating, `delivery` for the final; paid plan: `cloud render --fps <data-fps> --quality high -o out.mp4`). Confirm the file is non-empty and its `ffprobe` duration matches the root `data-duration`, then look at decoded frames.

"This element" or the current selection: `npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields selection`; `no-selection` means ask them to click it.

## Edit the timeline

These are the edits Studio itself makes, so the result stays in Studio's shape.

- `timeline --json` lists clips with absolute `absStart`/`absEnd`, owning `file` and the `#id` ref the edit commands take (`timeline ids` stamps missing ids).
- `timeline move|trim|split|set|duplicate|delete <ref> … --plan --json` previews one edit; run it again without `--plan`. `--start`, `--end`, `--duration` set one edge or the length.
- An edit is refused when the clip would overlap a neighbour (`--overwrite`, or move the neighbour first) or end past its composition: raise the root's `data-duration` first. No command changes `data-duration`.
- Several edits at once: a JSON file such as `[{"verb": "move", "ref": "#outro", "time": "9"}]`, then `timeline apply plan.json --json`. Each run prints a `receipt`; save it and `timeline undo receipt.json` reverts it.

<!-- history (trial): remove this block together with the command -->

## Project history

Every write is kept and can be undone. At the start of a turn, `npx hyperframes history begin --who <you> --label "<plan>"`, then `history --since mine --who <you>` to see what the person changed; build on their edits. A check failed or they say it got worse: `history undo --who <you>`, never hand-edit back. End the turn with `history end`.

<!-- /history (trial) -->

## Render where

| Need | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Local | `render --quality looks -o out.mp4` (`draft`, `delivery`) |
| Reproducible container | `render --docker --strict -o out.mp4` |
| Batch from variables | `render --batch rows.json -o "renders/{name}.mp4"` |
| Hosted, no local Chrome or FFmpeg | `cloud render` (`references/cloud.md`) |
| Your own AWS or GCP | `lambda render`, `cloudrun render` (`references/lambda.md`, `references/cloudrun.md`) |

A 30 s film renders in a minute or two: run it in the foreground. Detach only a render longer than your tool's timeout (`HYPERFRAMES_RENDER_DETACHED=1`, its own group, output to a log) and wait with `until grep -qE 'Render (complete|failed)' render.log; do sleep 5; done`, never `pgrep -f`, which matches its own loop and waits until the tool times out.

After a verified render, send one `feedback --rating`, plus a report for anything the person asked for that HyperFrames can't do, unless telemetry is off: `references/feedback.md`.

## When a command fails

| Symptom | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Chrome missing or won't start | `npx hyperframes browser ensure`; `doctor --json` always exits 0, gate on `.ok` |
| A heavy page isn't ready in time | Raise `--timeout` on `check` or `snapshot` |
| Unusual codec looks blank | Keep `--proxy` on (the default) |
| Render slow on Linux | The summary's second line says `screenshot` + `software gpu`: the slow path |
| `capture` fails or writes `BLOCKED.md` | Take nothing from its partial files; retry into a new `-o` folder |
| Disk tight | `clean --dry-run`, then `clean`; never delete `.hyperframes` (it holds history) |

## References

Read the row before running its command.

| Commands | Read |
| --- | --- |
| `init`, `capture`, `skills` | `references/init-and-scaffold.md` |
| `lint`, `check`, motion sidecars, `snapshot` | `references/lint-validate-inspect.md` |
| `compare`, `grade-compare`, `render --batch` | `references/compare-and-batch.md` |
| `beats` | `references/beats.md` |
| `preview`, `play`, `render`, `publish`, Studio context | `references/preview-render.md` |
| `doctor`, `browser` | `references/doctor-browser.md` |
| `auth`, `cloud`, template variables | `references/cloud.md` |
| `lambda`, `cloudrun` | `references/lambda.md`, `references/cloudrun.md` |
| `info`, `upgrade`, `compositions`, `timeline`, `docs`, `usage`, telemetry | `references/upgrade-info-misc.md` |
| `--strict` flags, run ids, `clean`, shader lint, JSON paths | `references/conventions.md` |
| `keyframes` | `../hyperframes/references/motion.md` (Seeing motion) |

<skill_content name="hyperframes">
# Skill: hyperframes

**Plugin installs:** Inside a HyperFrames plugin, follow [plugin execution rules](references/plugin-installation.md).

**Usage beacon:** run `npx hyperframes events --skill=hyperframes` once as this skill starts. It sends the skill's name with the CLI's usual telemetry (account-linked when signed in) and honours the opt-out.

# HyperFrames

HyperFrames renders HTML to video by seeking a paused timeline frame by frame, so every render is identical; the person edits the same files in the Studio preview. Use it unless another framework or a plain browser recording is asked for. Run the CLI as `npx hyperframes <command>` (`/hyperframes-cli`); at the start of a new video, `npx hyperframes usage --json` reports the person's remaining plan usage (say "unknown" when it is).

`index.html` is the root composition: it declares the video's variables and mounts one scene per sub-composition from `compositions/`. Media and fonts live in `assets/`. A new project: `npx hyperframes init <dir> --skip-skills --skill=hyperframes`. A website as the subject: `npx hyperframes capture <url> --json`.

Build what was asked: no voiceover or captions and no new aspect ratio unless the request or the source calls for them; a film over ~15 s that tells something gets music and sound on its visible actions unless the person asked for silence (`references/sound.md`). A new video is 1920×1080 at 30 fps. A question, a hold or a loose idea gets an answer or a proposal, not an edit. Before hand-writing a named effect, transition, caption style, chart or card, search the registry (`/hyperframes-registry`). Any media (a presenter or avatar, footage, voice, music): `/media-use`, which says when HeyGen is needed and what is free. Show real things from their source (the product's screens, the brand's logo, a real place's imagery); draw only what has none.

## Contract

`npx hyperframes check --json` reports most violations with a `Fix:` line.

1. Every timed element has `class="clip"`, `data-start` and `data-duration` in seconds, and shows over `[start, start + duration)`: land an end state just before its end. `data-track-index` is only a Studio lane; paint order is `z-index`.
2. The video's length is the root's `data-duration`: overrun is cut, an early end holds the last frame.
3. Each composition builds one paused timeline and registers it after its tweens: `window.__timelines["<data-composition-id>"] = tl`.
4. No `Date.now()`, unseeded `Math.random()`, network fetches, timers or `repeat: -1`. Everything visible is a function of timeline time.
5. Never tween `display`, `visibility` or `autoAlpha` on a `.clip`; animate a child.
6. No CSS `transform` on an element GSAP transforms; animate transforms, not `left`/`top`/`width`/`height`.
7. Never `play()`, `pause()` or seek media. A `<video>` keeps its sound with `data-has-audio="true"`, else it is `muted`; music, voice, replacement sound and J/L cuts are a separate `<audio>`.
8. Every `<audio>` has an `id` or it is left out of the mix. No `crossorigin` on media. Time the `<video>`, never its wrapper.
9. Only the bundled fonts (`references/format.md`) resolve by name; any other family needs `@font-face` to a file in `assets/fonts/`.
10. Asset paths: `assets/...` (no leading `/`), in sub-compositions too.
11. Grades, grain, blur and vignettes on footage go through `npx hyperframes media-treatment` (`/media-use`), never CSS filters.
12. A scene file puts its styles, markup and scripts inside `<template>` and styles its root as `#root`. Intended overflow or overlap: `data-layout-allow-overflow`, `data-layout-allow-overlap`.

## Keep it editable

Studio edits the tags you write.

- One scene per sub-composition, short readable ids; the root holds only scene hosts, media and audio.
- Timed elements are written in the HTML, not made by script, each with a stable `id`.
- Copy, brand colours and swappable media are variables (`data-var-text`, `data-var-src`, `var(--id)`).
- One kind per track: `data-track-kind="graphics"` on scene and overlay hosts, `captions` on the one host that holds every caption group.
- Content stays inside the 90% action-safe box, captions and key text inside 80% title-safe; Studio draws the guides, never add them.

## Work loop

- An existing project: `npx hyperframes timeline --json` shows what plays when; before any change, `npx hyperframes history --since mine --who <you>` shows what the person changed since your last turn: build on it (`/hyperframes-cli`).
- A new film over ~15 s that tells something: its type's file (below), then `references/story.md`: three storylines that are three different films, in words only; the person picks unless they asked for the file or no stops. Then `SPEC.md` (`references/spec.md`): every adjective as a number, the defaults banned by name, the shots by frame.
- After your last edit: `npx hyperframes check --json`; fix every error, weigh every warning. A film: `npx hyperframes snapshot --review` and `references/review.md`, ending in `REVIEW.md`. A small edit: snapshot what you changed (`--at`, `--range`, `--composition`) and look before you reply.
- Render when the person approves the Studio preview, asks for the file or asks for no stops, after your check and review pass; otherwise stop at the preview and wait.

## The HyperFrames desktop app

Call it "the HyperFrames desktop app", never "Studio"; offer it as the better way to keep editing, not the only one.

- Before the delivery render of a new video, open the Studio preview, even in no-questions mode, and say they can edit there. If `preview` printed "Keep editing by chatting with Framey", add that the **Edit with Framey** button opens the app.
- After the delivery render, pass on its Framey line in your own words: offer to run the `hyperframes open` it names or give its download link; else say nothing (autonomous: the delivery note).
- When any command says to run `catch-up`, run `npx hyperframes catch-up [dir]` before your next change; what it lists is their work, not a new request.

## What to read

| The request | Read |
| --- | --- |
| A video to copy or remake | `/reverse-any-video` |
| An episode in a proven style | `/style-sampling` |
| Another film's style on a new topic | `references/look.md` |
| Launch, promo, feature | `references/types/launch.md` |
| Explainer, tutorial | `references/types/explainer.md` |
| Music video | `references/types/music.md` |
| Chart, numbers | `references/types/data.md` |
| Vertical or social clip | `references/types/vertical.md` |
| 3D, simulation, generative | `references/types/3d.md` |
| Character, mascot, story short | `references/types/character.md` |
| A real place or map; a website, PR or script; kinetic type | `references/film.md` |
| Captions; cards over a talking head | `references/captions.md`; `references/overlays.md` |
| Motion: eases, titles, cuts, punch-ins, speed, holds | `references/motion.md` |
| Scenes, attributes, media, lint; GSAP, Lottie, 3D, canvas | `references/format.md`; `references/runtimes.md` |

# Skill: hyperframes-cli

**Plugin installs:** Inside a HyperFrames plugin, follow [plugin execution rules](../hyperframes/references/plugin-installation.md).

**Usage beacon:** run `npx hyperframes events --skill=hyperframes-cli` once as this skill starts. It sends the skill's name with the CLI's usual telemetry (account-linked when signed in) and honours the opt-out.

# HyperFrames CLI

Run `npx hyperframes <command>` unless the project gives a wrapper; then use the wrapper. It needs Node.js 22+ and FFmpeg. Every command has `--help`; most take `--json`, and a failure prints `✗ …`, a `Fix:` line and exits non-zero.

A `--json` result may carry `_meta.updateNotice`: a newer HyperFrames release is out. Pass it to the person once per conversation, in your own words, at a natural pause; updating is theirs to decide.

## Commands by job

| Job | Commands |
| --- | --- |
| Start | `init <dir> --skip-skills` (blank; `--example <name>` only when asked), `capture <url>` |
| Read a project | `info`, `compositions`, `timeline --json`, `docs <topic>` |
| Check it | `lint` while writing; `check --json` as the gate (lint, runtime, layout, contrast) |
| Look at it | `snapshot` (`--at <t,…>`, `--range START,END`, `--composition <id>`, `--zoom`, `--angle`, `--against <video>`), `keyframes`, `compare`, `audio` |
| Edit the timeline | `timeline` with `move`, `trim`, `split`, `set`, `duplicate`, `delete`, `apply`, `undo`, `ids` |
| Reuse | `catalog`, `add` (`/hyperframes-registry`) |
| Media and sound | `media-treatment`, `grade-compare`, `remove-background`, `tts`, `transcribe`, `beats`, `normalize-audio` (`/media-use`) |
| Show and ship | `preview`, `present` (`/slideshow`), `render`, `publish`, `cloud`, `lambda`, `cloudrun` |
| Desktop app | `open`, `catch-up` |
| Upkeep | `doctor`, `browser`, `upgrade`, `usage`, `clean`, `feedback` |

`captions` is not a command: run `transcribe`, then read ../hyperframes/references/captions.md.

`validate`, `inspect` and `layout` are deprecated aliases of `check`; `events` is skills' own telemetry. Don't run them.

## The loop

1. Write, then `npx hyperframes lint` after the first pass and after structural changes.
2. `npx hyperframes check --json` and fix every error. While a lint error remains the layout and contrast audits don't run; "0 samples" means nothing was checked. Contrast failures carry a `suggestedColor`. A finding at a single sample (an entrance in flight) is info; a 3 s+ video with no visible change fails `sweep_static`.
3. `npx hyperframes snapshot` and read the PNGs (under `.hyperframes/artifacts/snapshots/`): that is how you see the video. With sub-compositions, snapshot a midpoint of every scene; tiny unstyled content or a missing hero is a mount defect (`../hyperframes/references/format.md`).
4. `npx hyperframes preview --background`, check the URL answers 200, give the person the project URL and wait, unless they asked for the file or for no stops. Passing checks alone is not a reason to render.
5. Time to render (step 4): `npx hyperframes render --quality looks -o out.mp4` (`draft` while iterating, `delivery` for the final; paid plan: `cloud render --fps <data-fps> --quality high -o out.mp4`). Confirm the file is non-empty and its `ffprobe` duration matches the root `data-duration`, then look at decoded frames.

"This element" or the current selection: `npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields selection`; `no-selection` means ask them to click it.

## Edit the timeline

These are the edits Studio itself makes, so the result stays in Studio's shape.

- `timeline --json` lists clips with absolute `absStart`/`absEnd`, owning `file` and the `#id` ref the edit commands take (`timeline ids` stamps missing ids).
- `timeline move|trim|split|set|duplicate|delete <ref> … --plan --json` previews one edit; run it again without `--plan`. `--start`, `--end`, `--duration` set one edge or the length.
- An edit is refused when the clip would overlap a neighbour (`--overwrite`, or move the neighbour first) or end past its composition: raise the root's `data-duration` first. No command changes `data-duration`.
- Several edits at once: a JSON file such as `[{"verb": "move", "ref": "#outro", "time": "9"}]`, then `timeline apply plan.json --json`. Each run prints a `receipt`; save it and `timeline undo receipt.json` reverts it.

<!-- history (trial): remove this block together with the command -->

## Project history

Every write is kept and can be undone. At the start of a turn, `npx hyperframes history begin --who <you> --label "<plan>"`, then `history --since mine --who <you>` to see what the person changed; build on their edits. A check failed or they say it got worse: `history undo --who <you>`, never hand-edit back. End the turn with `history end`.

<!-- /history (trial) -->

## Render where

| Need | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Local | `render --quality looks -o out.mp4` (`draft`, `delivery`) |
| Reproducible container | `render --docker --strict -o out.mp4` |
| Batch from variables | `render --batch rows.json -o "renders/{name}.mp4"` |
| Hosted, no local Chrome or FFmpeg | `cloud render` (`references/cloud.md`) |
| Your own AWS or GCP | `lambda render`, `cloudrun render` (`references/lambda.md`, `references/cloudrun.md`) |

A 30 s film renders in a minute or two: run it in the foreground. Detach only a render longer than your tool's timeout (`HYPERFRAMES_RENDER_DETACHED=1`, its own group, output to a log) and wait with `until grep -qE 'Render (complete|failed)' render.log; do sleep 5; done`, never `pgrep -f`, which matches its own loop and waits until the tool times out.

After a verified render, send one `feedback --rating`, plus a report for anything the person asked for that HyperFrames can't do, unless telemetry is off: `references/feedback.md`.

## When a command fails

| Symptom | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Chrome missing or won't start | `npx hyperframes browser ensure`; `doctor --json` always exits 0, gate on `.ok` |
| A heavy page isn't ready in time | Raise `--timeout` on `check` or `snapshot` |
| Unusual codec looks blank | Keep `--proxy` on (the default) |
| Render slow on Linux | The summary's second line says `screenshot` + `software gpu`: the slow path |
| `capture` fails or writes `BLOCKED.md` | Take nothing from its partial files; retry into a new `-o` folder |
| Disk tight | `clean --dry-run`, then `clean`; never delete `.hyperframes` (it holds history) |

## References

Read the row before running its command.

| Commands | Read |
| --- | --- |
| `init`, `capture`, `skills` | `references/init-and-scaffold.md` |
| `lint`, `check`, motion sidecars, `snapshot` | `references/lint-validate-inspect.md` |
| `compare`, `grade-compare`, `render --batch` | `references/compare-and-batch.md` |
| `beats` | `references/beats.md` |
| `preview`, `play`, `render`, `publish`, Studio context | `references/preview-render.md` |
| `doctor`, `browser` | `references/doctor-browser.md` |
| `auth`, `cloud`, template variables | `references/cloud.md` |
| `lambda`, `cloudrun` | `references/lambda.md`, `references/cloudrun.md` |
| `info`, `upgrade`, `compositions`, `timeline`, `docs`, `usage`, telemetry | `references/upgrade-info-misc.md` |
| `--strict` flags, run ids, `clean`, shader lint, JSON paths | `references/conventions.md` |
| `keyframes` | `../hyperframes/references/motion.md` (Seeing motion) |

1: # Explainers, tutorials and "how it works"
2: 
3: One idea the viewer understands by the end (`../story.md` §1). The spine is one concrete example worked through, start to finish, not a tour of facts. Usually 30–90 s.
4: 
5: ## Ground it first
6: 
7: Start where the viewer already is: a person, a place or a situation they know, and a question they would ask about it ("why does the astronaut come home younger than her twin?"). The abstract device (a light clock, a graph, a field) enters inside that situation, as the thing that answers the question, and the film returns to the person at the end with the answer. A film that opens on the device alone is a diagram, not an explainer.
8: 
9: ## Devices that explain
10: 
11: - **The object is the explanation.** Build a thing whose working is the idea: a machine, a model, a map, a light clock, drawn so it reads as what it is (its material, its mount, where it sits in the scene). Every number on screen comes from it, and the camera tours through it: cutaways, an exploded view, a dive into the part that matters.
12: - **One diagram that grows.** Start from the simplest true picture and add one part per beat, each appearing when it is named; never a finished diagram dropped on screen at once.
13: - **Continuous transformation.** Each step morphs out of the last (a bar becomes an axis, a dot becomes a population), so the viewer never loses the thread to a cut.
14: - **The worked example.** One real input (a sentence, a number, a photo) travels through every step to the answer.
15: 
16: ## Shapes of information
17: 
18: Most explainable lines are one of a few shapes, and each has its own picture: a number that lands (`data.md`); a myth turned over (the wrong idea struck through, the right one printed over it); before and after; many things converging into a few groups; a network that densifies; one chosen out of many; steps in order; a real screenshot with the detail circled; a quote set as a poster; a chapter card. Pick the shape first, then the picture, so similar lines get different pictures and every line gets the one that shows it.
19: 
20: ## Words
21: 
22: - Narrated: the voice is the clock (`../sound.md` §2). Reveal each part when the voice names it, across the back half of the scene; keep a scene to about 19 spoken words (`../film.md` "Script and pacing").
23: - Not narrated: large lines carry it, up to about 10 words, each held 0.5 s + 0.3 s a word.
24: - Labels sit on the part they name, with a leader line when needed, and appear with it. No legends, no bullet slides.
25: 
26: ## Getting it right
27: 
28: - Every claim, value and step traces to the source; a number the source did not give is left out or marked illustrative. One data module drives every figure so the numbers agree with each other.
29: - Check the science or the logic of each step before animating it; a beautiful wrong diagram is worse than none.
30: - End on the one idea in one line. No brand end card unless asked.
31: 
32: ## Tells for this type
33: 
34: A slide of bullets; icons in circles; three cards in a row; the whole diagram at once; a narrator repeating the text on screen word for word.

Read file .agents/skills/hyperframes/references/story.md, lines 1-103
1: # Story
2: 
3: Read before building any video that tells something over about 15 s: a launch or promo, an explainer, a pull-request or changelog video, a recap, a music video with a narrative. Most weak films are good motion around no story: a list of features, three cards in a row, a logo, a URL.
4: 
5: Skip it for an edit to an existing project, captions or overlays on footage, and a short single-idea piece (one kinetic line, a map move, a highlight on an image), where the request is the story. When the person gave a script, a storyboard or a reference film, follow theirs. The shape of each kind of film (launch, explainer, music, data, vertical, 3D, character) is in `types/`.
6: 
7: ## 1. The one thing
8: 
9: - **What it is**, in one line: "You can now …" for a launch, the one idea the viewer must understand for an explainer, what changed and why it matters for a pull request. A whole release ("2.0", "what's new") is not one thing: take its headline.
10: - **The one thing to remember** after the film ends, in the viewer's words, not the brand slogan.
11: - **One viewer doing one real task**, from the moment they need it to the result. That task is the spine, and one real piece of data (a query, a file, a prompt, a number) travels through it from the hook to the payoff. An explainer's spine is one concrete example worked through.
12: - Keep facts (what it does, real numbers, real labels) apart from creative choices (angle, tone, look). Every claim on screen traces to the source: the site, the PR, the docs or the person's words. Use the person's own copy verbatim.
13: - What the source does not say stays unsaid: never derive a claim it did not make ("40 min to 2 min" is not "20× faster"), mark an example number as illustrative, and show a screen you cannot get as a labelled placeholder, not a drawn one.
14: 
15: ## 2. Three storylines, then one
16: 
17: Write three. They are three different films, not three titles on one film: each has its own **world** (where it happens and what it looks like), its own **device** (what the story is) and its own **form** (how the camera and the cuts carry it). Sketch five or more ideas first, a line each pairing a device with a form (tables below); drop those the subject cannot carry well, and of the rest keep the three that differ most. Make one of the three the bold one you would not have picked first. Each says:
18: 
19: - its name, its device and form in a few words, and in two sentences what the viewer sees and feels;
20: - the first two seconds, exactly;
21: - its beats in one line (`hook → … → end card`);
22: - its look in one line: ground, type, the one material or treatment, taken from the subject or the brand (`look.md`);
23: - its sound in one line (`sound.md` §1).
24: 
25: The storylines are words: build nothing for any of them before one is picked. Pick a storyline for its story: the one a stranger would follow and remember, with people or a situation they know, ahead of the most striking picture. Picking a storyline picks its look and its sound. Then write the picked one as `SPEC.md`.
26: 
27: Put your recommendation first, with the reason in one clause, and save all three in the project as `STORYLINES.md` so a later turn can switch.
28: 
29: - **The person is there to answer:** show the three and stop once until they pick. A mix ("A's opening with C's middle") is one storyline. Ask nothing else unless only they can answer it (real screens you cannot capture, narrated or music only). State everything else in one assumption line: the length as a range, the aspect, music or voice, and every paid item (a HeyGen voice, an avatar, catalog music) with the free option beside it.
30: - **They asked for the file or for no stops:** take your recommendation, build it, and name the other two in one line each in your reply.
31: - With a storyboard (`storyboard.md`), the picked storyline becomes the board's frames.
32: 
33: | Device                        | What the viewer sees                                                                    |
34: | ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
35: | A moment in someone's day     | a person, a time stamp, the message that creates the need ("launch is tomorrow")        |
36: | A character does the work     | a mascot or a cursor carries, drags, draws and reacts; every cut has a cause            |
37: | The feature as the hook       | the feature happening to a recognisable image in the first half second                  |
38: | The result first              | the finished output plays, then the camera pulls back to show where it came from        |
39: | One object across apps        | the thing being made travels from one app into the product, which keeps working on it   |
40: | Life before and after         | the old way as a scene (one person drowning in tabs), then the new way                  |
41: | Type carries the argument     | giant kinetic type, colour fields and grids that cut on the beat                        |
42: | A number lands                | one real number earned by a scene, then made physical                                   |
43: | A question with the input     | "What if you could make a video from your ⟨website⟩?", the blank filled by a real input |
44: | The object is the explanation | a machine or model whose working is the idea; the camera tours through it               |
45: 
46: | Form                       | What the viewer sees                                                                         |
47: | -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
48: | One continuous take        | the camera never cuts; it pushes, pulls and travels from one world into the next             |
49: | Object-to-object chain     | every shot ends on the thing that opens the next: a button becomes a card becomes a phone    |
50: | An endless zoom            | the camera dives into a detail that turns out to be the next world, again and again          |
51: | A flight through one world | a 3D set, a map or a desk the camera travels across; each idea is a stop on the route        |
52: | Cut on the beat            | hard cuts on the music, type and colour fields changing every half beat                      |
53: | Match cuts                 | one shape holds while everything around it changes: a circle becomes a lens, a wheel, a logo |
54: | Split screen to one        | several panes play at once, then collapse into the one that matters                          |
55: | One frame that rebuilds    | a single composition keeps rearranging itself and never leaves the frame                     |
56: 
57: A pitch where all three are plain cuts between scenes has not tried the forms. Before and after: the new side moves calmly while the old side churns; never mock a named competitor. A recap asks one question first so each piece answers it.
58: 
59: ## 3. The hook
60: 
61: The first two seconds are the densest of the film, and frame 0 is the thumbnail: never black, never a logo alone. Open on the feature working on something recognisable, a real moment that creates the need, a question with the input inside it, a sentence whose last word becomes the picture, or the bug itself. Then let the old way fail on screen (the wait, the wall of text, the wrong result) before the product brings relief; the proof is often the same shot improved in front of the viewer. Typing into a prompt box as the opener, with nothing else on screen, is the tell of a generated film; as a story step a few seconds in, it is fine.
62: 
63: ## 4. Beats
64: 
65: A common shape for a launch of about 35 s; scale it, let the device bend it, and take another type's shape from its file in `types/`:
66: 
67: | Beat     | Share | Job                                                                                       |
68: | -------- | ----- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
69: | Hook     | ~8%   | the world and the need, or the feature already working                                    |
70: | Tension  | ~12%  | the old way failing on screen, or a gag                                                   |
71: | Reveal   | ~8%   | the product or idea named as a title, about 20–30% in                                     |
72: | Proof    | ~40%  | the real task in the real UI as 3–6 verbs (_paste, pick, watch it build, ship_), one each |
73: | Payoff   | ~20%  | the output arrives, already moving: the biggest visual moment, once, 60–80% in            |
74: | Claim    | ~8%   | the one thing, in one line                                                                |
75: | End card | ~8%   | the mark carried in, the name and the call to action land and hold 2–3 s                  |
76: 
77: In each verb beat keep only what the cursor touches and what proves the line; delete the rest of the screen. The process runs fast; the payoff plays at normal speed. Length follows the story (a feature launch is usually 20–45 s); a length in the request is a range, never padded.
78: 
79: ## 5. Worlds
80: 
81: A film visits several worlds, each with its own background, light and scale (a desktop, the product on a brand gradient, a white void with a character, live action), never one dark canvas with small UI floating in it. Enter each world through an object already on screen: the thing clicked becomes the next shot. Keep one home stage to return to, one carrier the eye follows, and the palette and type constant across worlds.
82: 
83: ## 6. Copy and voice
84: 
85: - Titles take at most 6 words a line, one line on screen at a time, no trailing periods; an explainer's lines may run to about 10. A line holds about 0.3 s a word plus 0.5 s, and the last line at least 2 s.
86: - Show, don't list: no bullet slides or three-card rows. When similar things repeat, each gets its own idea and layout.
87: - Real numbers only, from the source. The first line is never "Introducing", "Meet" or the logo; after the pain, "Introducing X" is fine. Never "unlock", "seamless", "supercharge", "game-changer", "revolutionize", "effortless", or "in seconds" unless measured.
88: - Read the lines alone: a stranger gets the pitch. Watch the pictures alone: they tell the same story.
89: - No voiceover unless the request or the source calls for one; then the screen never repeats the spoken sentence word for word. Without a voice, large titles and the product's own text carry the words, over music and effects (`sound.md`).
90: 
91: ## 7. The brand
92: 
93: The mark lands once, with weight, usually on the end card; before it the brand shows only inside the product and the story, never docked small in a corner. The end card is built, not a still: the mark is carried in, typed or wiped in. The accent colour is rationed: one highlighted word, the payoff, the end card.
94: 
95: ## 8. Tells of a generated film
96: 
97: The defaults a film falls into when nothing is decided are banned by name in `spec.md` ("BANNED by default"): a dark void with small things floating in it, glow and particles, the cream-paper-serif-mono-label look, everything fading and sliding up, three cards in a row, the docked logo. Beyond those, for a story:
98: 
99: - every scene entering the same way, or the same move beat after beat;
100: - side-by-side panels and floating cards standing in for a scene;
101: - titles that keep sliding or shrinking after they land; breathing or floating loops standing in for motion on titles and UI (a character's idle breath is acting, `types/character.md`).
102: 
103: When a first render shows any of them, name which, take the replacement from the subject, the brand or the medium, and add it to the BANNED line of `SPEC.md`.

Read file .agents/skills/hyperframes/references/spec.md, lines 1-76
1: # The spec
2: 
3: Adjectives are where the default look lives. Given "premium, modern, clean", the model fills every gap with its own defaults, and they look the same in every run: a dark void, a glow, small type floating in the middle, everything fading in. Every adjective you turn into a number is a decision taken back from those defaults.
4: 
5: So before any scene, write `SPEC.md` at the project root: the film as a director's brief to yourself, with a number wherever you would have written an adjective. Build from it, check against it, and change it when a review changes the film.
6: 
7: The spec serves the story, never the other way round (`story.md`). A look that turns the story's things into abstract shapes has failed, however striking the frame.
8: 
9: ## The template
10: 
11: ```text
12: GOAL:    what the viewer feels or does at the end, one sentence
13: OUTPUT:  HyperFrames, W x H, fps
14: TIME:    seconds x fps = frames; BPM and frames per beat when there is music
15: LOOK:    ground (hex, texture and its amount), ink, one accent and where it may appear;
16:          display face + weight + size in px + tracking, body face the same;
17:          the medium (paper and ink, photographs, product UI, glass, clay, 3D studio) with its numbers;
18:          light and depth: shadow offset, blur and opacity, grain %, vignette %
19: OBJECTS: every thing the story needs the viewer to recognise (a mirror, a clock, a phone, a person),
20:          drawn with the material and details that make it read without a label: a mirror is
21:          silvered glass with a bright edge and a mount, not a bar
22: MOTION:  eases by role as named curves (enter, move, exit, camera); springs as damping ratio;
23:          durations and staggers in frames
24: SHOTS:   one line per shot: frame range, the one hero move, what the viewer reads (with its window),
25:          the sound, and how it hands off to the next shot
26: BANNED:  the defaults below, plus anything this film must not become
27: QA:      the frames to check, and what each must show
28: ```
29: 
30: ## Turning words into numbers
31: 
32: | The word  | Becomes                                                                                                                                |
33: | --------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
34: | premium   | a material with numbers: satin paper with 2% grain, a product on a seamless sweep with a 0.55 contact shadow, chrome at roughness 0.05 |
35: | modern    | a camera and a type system: a 30-frame push on one ease, a display face at 9% of the frame height with -2% tracking                    |
36: | clean     | a grid and a ration: 12 columns, 96 px margins, the accent on one word per shot                                                        |
37: | dynamic   | cuts on the beat, a layout change on the bar (every 4 beats), one hero move per shot                                                   |
38: | playful   | springs at damping 0.45-0.6 on position and scale (never on opacity or colour), 10-30% exaggerated poses                               |
39: | cinematic | a lens and a light: a 35 mm framing, a key from upper left, a rim from behind, 6% vignette                                             |
40: 
41: ## Composition numbers
42: 
43: - The hero of a shot fills at least 40% of the frame's height or width. A small object in the middle of an empty frame is never a shot; push in, crop, or give it a world.
44: - One hero move per shot. Secondary moves travel 50-70% as far, start 100-200 ms after it, and everything else holds still.
45: - In a story film every shot moves the story: something happens that causes the next shot. Lines read as cause and effect ("so…", "which means…"), not slogans.
46: - An information card (B-roll over a talking head, a data beat, a vertical explainer card) is different: its information is on screen within about 2.5 s, then it holds, so any paused frame reads as a finished poster.
47: - Something new every 2-4 s across the film; a new layout every bar when there is music.
48: - Text meant to be read: at least 28 px at 1080 (2.6% of the short side), held 0.5 s + 0.3 s a word. Too many words: cut words, never shrink type.
49: 
50: ## BANNED by default
51: 
52: These are where generated video lands when nothing else is decided. Each is banned unless the brand's own material or the person's reference uses it, and then only as they use it:
53: 
54: - a black or dark navy void as the ground, with small elements floating in its middle;
55: - glow, bloom, neon, lens flares, glowing orbs and rings; floating particles as decoration;
56: - purple or blue gradients, mesh gradients, glass cards;
57: - a cream or off-white paper ground with a serif display, italic accent words, numbered "01 / 02" labels, small monospace caps labels, pill-shaped chips and buttons;
58: - everything centred; everything fading in at once; every element fading and sliding up;
59: - text that moves while it is read; titles that keep drifting after they land;
60: - corner labels, frame borders, corner brackets, HUD readouts as decoration;
61: - three cards in a row, KPI grids, a title over a dimmed screenshot;
62: - the logo docked in a corner.
63: 
64: After the first render, name every default it used anyway, from this list or not, add each to the film's BANNED line, and fix them. The list grows with every film.
65: 
66: ## A look built from a medium
67: 
68: A look holds together when it is the rules of one medium, not a palette. A risograph look, for example, is five parts and nothing else:
69: 
70: - **paper**: one flat colour with a fibre noise, no gradients;
71: - **ink A**: every word that must be read and every structural line;
72: - **ink B**: one fluorescent accent, one focus per frame (the number, the bar, the stamp);
73: - **overprint**: where the inks overlap a third colour appears, and the B plate sits 3 px off register;
74: - **halftone**: every gradient is dots.
75: 
76: Motion comes from the same medium: the frame is printed, plate by plate, not faded in. Write any look this way: its parts, what each may carry, and how the medium itself moves (paper is cut and lifted, ink is printed, glass refracts, clay is pressed).

Instructions from: /Users/alessandrojcm/repos/dhc-dashboard/videos/workshops/AGENTS.md
# HyperFrames Composition Project

This folder is a [HyperFrames](https://hyperframes.heygen.com) video: HTML, CSS and seekable
animations (GSAP by default) that the `hyperframes` CLI previews in the browser and renders to
MP4.

## Skills — read these first

**Invoke the relevant skill before writing or modifying compositions.** Skills encode framework-specific patterns (e.g., `window.__timelines` registration, `data-*` attribute semantics, shader-compatible CSS rules) that generic web docs don't cover, so compositions written without them break.

**Doing anything with HyperFrames?** Start at `/hyperframes`. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (each kind of film, story, motion, look, sound, review, captions, overlays). Read it first, especially when there's no project context to orient you.

- `/hyperframes` — read first for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays. Holds the render contract and the work loop.
- `/hyperframes-cli` — the CLI by job: scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render, publish, project history.
- `/hyperframes-registry` — ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source. Search it before hand-building any named visual.
- `/media-use` — get or make any media (music, sound effects, images, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades) and mix placed audio.
- `/reverse-any-video` — rebuild any video file as an editable HyperFrames project and check it against the original frame by frame (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/style-sampling` — make a new episode on your topic in one of five proven styles (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/figma` — bring a Figma design, frame, logo or brand into a video.
- `/slideshow` — a presentation or pitch deck. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4.
- `/remotion-to-hyperframes` — bring existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, or renders from other tools) and verify it frame by frame against the original.

**Changing how real footage or images look or reveal?** Load `/media-use` and read its `references/media-treatments.md` before editing, even when the request only says dark, flat, boring, retro, private, or “make the reveal cooler.” It governs how footage is treated, never whether media may be used. Use canonical media treatments and seek-safe motion; do not improvise equivalent CSS/SVG filters or overlays.

> **Tailwind v4 projects** (`hyperframes init --tailwind`): see `hyperframes-cli/references/init-and-scaffold.md` (Tailwind).

> **Using a HyperFrames plugin?** Load skills from that installed bundle and follow
> its `hyperframes/references/plugin-installation.md` execution rules. The person updates
> the plugin through its plugin manager; the standalone commands below do not apply.
>
> **Standalone skill missing or stale?** Installing and updating skills is the person's step:
> tell them which skill is missing or stale, and do not run the install yourself. For the user:
> `npx hyperframes skills update <name>` installs/refreshes that skill, and bare
> `npx hyperframes skills update` refreshes the core set plus everything already installed —
> neither pulls the full set. Newly installed skills load in a new agent session.

## Commands

```bash
npm run dev          # human-operated foreground preview (blocks until stopped)
npx hyperframes preview --background  # agent-safe persistent Studio preview
npx hyperframes preview --status      # verify the persistent preview is listening
npx hyperframes preview --stop        # stop it when review is finished
npm run check        # lint + runtime + layout + motion + contrast (one command)
npx hyperframes snapshot --at 1,3,5  # PNG frames at those seconds, to look at before rendering
npm run render       # render to MP4
npm run publish      # publish and get a shareable link
npx hyperframes lint --verbose  # include info-level findings
npx hyperframes lint --json     # machine-readable output for CI
npx hyperframes docs <topic> # reference docs in terminal
```

> **Agents must use `npx hyperframes preview --background` for Studio handoff.** Do not rely
> on a shell/tool `run_in_background` wrapper around `npm run dev`: that foreground process
> remains owned by the invoking session and can disappear while the browser stays open,
> leaving refreshes at `ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT`. Verify with `preview --status`. The desktop
> app can't edit the project while this preview runs, so `npx hyperframes open` stops it first.
> If you hand the project to the app another way, run `preview --stop` before you do. Otherwise keep it
> alive through review, and stop it explicitly with `preview --stop` afterward.

> **Back from the desktop app.** Once this project was opened in the HyperFrames desktop app, run `npx hyperframes catch-up` before your next change here: it lists what the person asked Framey in the app and which files changed since.

> **Pinned CLI version.** These scripts pin an exact `hyperframes@X.Y.Z` so this project re-renders identically over time. Weeks later that pin lags fixes shipped since. To move up: `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project . --check` (shows the delta), then `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project .` to rewrite the pins. Always unpinned — the pinned script re-runs the old version against itself.

## Documentation

**For quick reference**, use the local CLI docs command (no network required):

```bash
npx hyperframes docs <topic>
```

Topics: `data-attributes`, `gsap`, `compositions`, `rendering`, `examples`, `troubleshooting`

**For full documentation**, discover pages via the machine-readable index — do NOT guess URLs:

```
https://hyperframes.heygen.com/llms.txt
```

## Project Structure

- `index.html` — main composition (root timeline)
- `compositions/` — sub-compositions referenced via `data-composition-src`
- `meta.json` — project metadata (id, name)
- `transcript.json` — whisper word-level transcript (if generated)

## Linting — ALWAYS RUN AFTER CHANGES

After creating or editing any `.html` composition, **always** run the full check before considering the task complete:

```bash
npm run check
```

Fix all errors before presenting the result. Warnings should be reviewed before rendering.

Then look at what you changed: `npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>` (or `--range START,END`, `--composition <id>`) at the moments you edited, and read the frames before you reply. A passing check does not show how it looks.

## Key Rules

1. Every timed element needs `data-start` and a duration. `data-start` is what marks it as timed; `data-track-index` is an optional Studio display lane the render never reads
2. Give timed visual elements `class="clip"`. The framework keys visibility off `data-start`, not the class, but the shared `.clip` CSS is what gives a scene its full-frame box, and `lint` warns without it
3. Register one paused root timeline per composition on `window.__timelines`:
   ```js
   window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {};
   window.__timelines["composition-id"] = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
   ```
   Scene timelines manually added to this root must not be paused. A paused
   child does not advance when the root is seeked. The runtime activates
   registered composition siblings, not arbitrary nested scene timelines.
4. A video with sound keeps it on the `<video>` (`data-has-audio="true"`, no `muted`). Use a separate `<audio>` for music, voiceover, replacement audio, J/L cuts, or audio detached in Studio. Silent footage and b-roll: `muted`.
5. Sub-compositions use `data-composition-src="compositions/file.html"` to reference other HTML files
6. Only deterministic logic — no `Date.now()`, no `Math.random()`, no network fetches

### First-time quartermaster workflow

1. **Confirm access.** The Inventory dashboard requires the `inventory.manage` capability; all holders have equal authority. [inventory layout](apps/web/src/routes/dashboard/inventory/+layout.server.ts#L4-L10), [router](apps/phoenix/lib/dhc_web/router.ex#L245-L250)

2. **Set up the inventory structure first.**
   - In **Categories and properties**, create categories, then add the typed properties each item should carry: text, decimal, yes/no, or single-choice options. Mark required fields and optionally use a property in the generated item label. [categories page](apps/web/src/routes/dashboard/inventory/categories/[[categoryId]]/+page.svelte#L608-L702)
   - In **Containers**, create a root storage location, then nest locations as needed. The UI prevents selecting an item itself or a descendant as a parent; moving locations by drag-and-drop is supported. [containers page](apps/web/src/routes/dashboard/inventory/containers/+page.svelte#L72-L100), [#L489-L492]
   - Caveats: a category can only be deleted when no items use it; retiring properties/options can be refused until active values are cleared or migrated. Containers must have active children/items handled before archive or deletion; restoring requires the parent chain first. [categories](apps/web/src/routes/dashboard/inventory/categories/[[categoryId]]/+page.svelte#L1221-L1229), [#L149-L165]; [containers](apps/web/src/routes/dashboard/inventory/containers/+page.svelte#L113-L140)

3. **Add each physical item.** In **Items → New item**, choose a category and storage container, complete that category’s properties, and add optional handling notes. The label and permanent item code are generated by the system. [items page](apps/web/src/routes/dashboard/inventory/items/[[itemId]]/+page.svelte#L229-L281), [#L305-L439]

4. **Maintain the register.**
   - Search/filter items; open **Manage** to update properties/notes, move storage, change category, or manage maintenance. [items page](apps/web/src/routes/dashboard/inventory/items/[[itemId]]/+page.svelte#L510-L637), [#L1027-L1204]
   - Starting maintenance requires a reason; ending it can include a note, and maintenance history remains visible. [items page](apps/web/src/routes/dashboard/inventory/items/[[itemId]]/+page.svelte#L1207-L1337)
   - Archive items that need a retained record; permanently delete only history-free items. [items page](apps/web/src/routes/dashboard/inventory/items/[[itemId]]/+page.svelte#L915-L1005), [#L1344-L1369]
   - Do not move an item with a live loan. If an item returns faulty, record the return first, then start maintenance. [inventory workflow doc](docs/ale-276-mobile-inventory-and-loan-workflow-prototype.md#L51-L54), [#L99-L102]

### Loan workflow

1. **Use the shared Loan queue** for daily work: Requests, Ready for handover, Returns and overdue, and Open maintenance. It is a shared operational queue—not a personal assignment list. [loan queue](apps/web/src/routes/dashboard/inventory/loans/+page.svelte#L293-L418); [queue design](docs/agents/where-to-look.md#L63)

2. **Review requests.** Open a request, set approved start/due dates, optionally add a member-facing decision note, then **Approve** or **Reject**. Approving reserves the item and rejects competing pending requests for it. [loan queue](apps/web/src/routes/dashboard/inventory/loans/+page.svelte#L481-L528); [operator rules](apps/phoenix/lib/dhc/inventory/operator_loans.ex#L10-L16)

3. **Record the real handover.** From **Ready for handover**, check the physical item and select **Record checkout**. Checkout is only allowed during the approved date window and when the item is not in maintenance. For an early or late handover, update dates first rather than bypassing the rule. [loan queue](apps/web/src/routes/dashboard/inventory/loans/+page.svelte#L324-L344), [#L530-L588]; [operator rules](apps/phoenix/lib/dhc/inventory/operator_loans.ex#L21-L29)

4. **Record returns.** Checked-out and overdue loans appear in **Returns and overdue**. Open the card and select **Record return**; update the due date first if necessary. [loan queue](apps/web/src/routes/dashboard/inventory/loans/+page.svelte#L355-L366), [#L589-L617]

### Important loan caveats

- An operator cancels only an **approved** loan. A pending request is **rejected**; a checked-out item is closed by **returning** it. [operator rules](apps/phoenix/lib/dhc/inventory/operator_loans.ex#L17-L29)
- After checkout, the start date is immutable; the due date remains editable but cannot predate the handover day. [operator rules](apps/phoenix/lib/dhc/inventory/operator_loans.ex#L27-L29), [loan policy](apps/phoenix/lib/dhc/inventory/loan_policy.ex#L92-L101)
- Desktop drag-and-drop is only a shortcut: it opens the confirmation panel and does not itself change a loan. [loan queue](apps/web/src/routes/dashboard/inventory/loans/+page.svelte#L274-L279)
- There is no label-printing, QR/barcode, or scanner workflow in this release. [inventory workflow doc](docs/ale-276-mobile-inventory-and-loan-workflow-prototype.md#L56-L61)

defmodule Dhc.Inventory.OperatorLoans do @moduledoc """ ALE-296 (ALE-286a): the operator half of the loan lifecycle behind `Dhc.Inventory`. Where `Dhc.Inventory.MemberLoans` owns what a borrower may do to their own loan — request, cancel before checkout, read their history — this slice owns every decision an operator makes about someone else's: * **Approve.** The single fair decision point. Approval atomically reserves the item and rejects *all* competing pending requests with a system note, so allocation is exactly-once (story 35). Dates may be adjusted, and the container path is snapshotted here because approval is what entitles the borrower to know where to collect (story 15). * **Reject.** Closes a pending request with an operator note and reserves nothing. * **Operator cancel.** Distinct from the member's cancellation: it applies only to an *approved* loan (ALE-273). A pending request is rejected, and after checkout the member holds the item, so release is a return. * **Checkout.** Gated to an `approved` loan whose approved window contains today and whose item is out of maintenance. The operator updates the dates *first* for an early or late handover, so the record matches reality rather than being bent by the command (story 37). * **Return.** Releases the item immediately. There is no condition subdomain — faults route to notes or a maintenance period. * **Date edits.** The start is immutable once the item has physically changed hands; the due date stays editable, including after checkout (ALE-279 supersedes the earlier no-edits rule). ## Transitions, and nothing else `requested → approved | rejected`, `approved → checked_out | cancelled`, `checked_out → returned`. There are no lost or written-off states, no queues, entitlements, auto-approval, or revival of a closed loan. A command that finds the loan in the wrong state returns a domain reason naming the state it needed (`:not_pending`, `:not_approved`, `:not_checked_out`), never a generic failure. Approval, checkout, and return are *not* idempotent, unlike the member's cancellation: each has an allocation or custody side effect, so a caller has to be able to tell whether this particular call was the one that reserved the item or handed it over. ## Where the work happens Since GH-508 this module is a **facade**: every command is one `Dhc.Inventory.AvailabilityCommands.execute/2` call as an `{:operator, id}` actor, and that boundary owns the transaction, the item-before-loan lock order, the re-read under the lock, the date and window policy, the constraint translation, and the operator projection. Nothing about a transition is decided here; adding a rule to a command means adding it there, once, where the member and item commands share it. ## Notifications None, on purpose. ALE-298 attaches keyed notifications *after* these commands return, through `Dhc.Inventory.notify_loan_transition/2`. Wiring `Dhc.Notifications.create/2` here would create exactly the duplicate notification problem the keyed seam exists to prevent. content.text:
Instructions from: /Users/alessandrojcm/repos/dhc-dashboard/videos/inventory/AGENTS.md
# HyperFrames Composition Project

This folder is a [HyperFrames](https://hyperframes.heygen.com) video: HTML, CSS and seekable
animations (GSAP by default) that the `hyperframes` CLI previews in the browser and renders to
MP4.

## Skills — read these first

**Invoke the relevant skill before writing or modifying compositions.** Skills encode framework-specific patterns (e.g., `window.__timelines` registration, `data-*` attribute semantics, shader-compatible CSS rules) that generic web docs don't cover, so compositions written without them break.

**Doing anything with HyperFrames?** Start at `/hyperframes`. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (each kind of film, story, motion, look, sound, review, captions, overlays). Read it first, especially when there's no project context to orient you.

- `/hyperframes` — read first for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays. Holds the render contract and the work loop.
- `/hyperframes-cli` — the CLI by job: scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render, publish, project history.
- `/hyperframes-registry` — ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source. Search it before hand-building any named visual.
- `/media-use` — get or make any media (music, sound effects, images, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades) and mix placed audio.
- `/reverse-any-video` — rebuild any video file as an editable HyperFrames project and check it against the original frame by frame (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/style-sampling` — make a new episode on your topic in one of five proven styles (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/figma` — bring a Figma design, frame, logo or brand into a video.
- `/slideshow` — a presentation or pitch deck. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4.
- `/remotion-to-hyperframes` — bring existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, or renders from other tools) and verify it frame by frame against the original.

**Changing how real footage or images look or reveal?** Load `/media-use` and read its `references/media-treatments.md` before editing, even when the request only says dark, flat, boring, retro, private, or “make the reveal cooler.” It governs how footage is treated, never whether media may be used. Use canonical media treatments and seek-safe motion; do not improvise equivalent CSS/SVG filters or overlays.

> **Tailwind v4 projects** (`hyperframes init --tailwind`): see `hyperframes-cli/references/init-and-scaffold.md` (Tailwind).

> **Using a HyperFrames plugin?** Load skills from that installed bundle and follow
> its `hyperframes/references/plugin-installation.md` execution rules. The person updates
> the plugin through its plugin manager; the standalone commands below do not apply.
>
> **Standalone skill missing or stale?** Installing and updating skills is the person's step:
> tell them which skill is missing or stale, and do not run the install yourself. For the user:
> `npx hyperframes skills update <name>` installs/refreshes that skill, and bare
> `npx hyperframes skills update` refreshes the core set plus everything already installed —
> neither pulls the full set. Newly installed skills load in a new agent session.

## Commands

```bash
npm run dev          # human-operated foreground preview (blocks until stopped)
npx hyperframes preview --background  # agent-safe persistent Studio preview
npx hyperframes preview --status      # verify the persistent preview is listening
npx hyperframes preview --stop        # stop it when review is finished
npm run check        # lint + runtime + layout + motion + contrast (one command)
npx hyperframes snapshot --at 1,3,5  # PNG frames at those seconds, to look at before rendering
npm run render       # render to MP4
npm run publish      # publish and get a shareable link
npx hyperframes lint --verbose  # include info-level findings
npx hyperframes lint --json     # machine-readable output for CI
npx hyperframes docs <topic> # reference docs in terminal
```

> **Agents must use `npx hyperframes preview --background` for Studio handoff.** Do not rely
> on a shell/tool `run_in_background` wrapper around `npm run dev`: that foreground process
> remains owned by the invoking session and can disappear while the browser stays open,
> leaving refreshes at `ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT`. Verify with `preview --status`. The desktop
> app can't edit the project while this preview runs, so `npx hyperframes open` stops it first.
> If you hand the project to the app another way, run `preview --stop` before you do. Otherwise keep it
> alive through review, and stop it explicitly with `preview --stop` afterward.

> **Back from the desktop app.** Once this project was opened in the HyperFrames desktop app, run `npx hyperframes catch-up` before your next change here: it lists what the person asked Framey in the app and which files changed since.

> **Pinned CLI version.** These scripts pin an exact `hyperframes@X.Y.Z` so this project re-renders identically over time. Weeks later that pin lags fixes shipped since. To move up: `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project . --check` (shows the delta), then `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project .` to rewrite the pins. Always unpinned — the pinned script re-runs the old version against itself.

## Documentation

**For quick reference**, use the local CLI docs command (no network required):

```bash
npx hyperframes docs <topic>
```

Topics: `data-attributes`, `gsap`, `compositions`, `rendering`, `examples`, `troubleshooting`

**For full documentation**, discover pages via the machine-readable index — do NOT guess URLs:

```
https://hyperframes.heygen.com/llms.txt
```

## Project Structure

- `index.html` — main composition (root timeline)
- `compositions/` — sub-compositions referenced via `data-composition-src`
- `meta.json` — project metadata (id, name)
- `transcript.json` — whisper word-level transcript (if generated)

## Linting — ALWAYS RUN AFTER CHANGES

After creating or editing any `.html` composition, **always** run the full check before considering the task complete:

```bash
npm run check
```

Fix all errors before presenting the result. Warnings should be reviewed before rendering.

Then look at what you changed: `npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>` (or `--range START,END`, `--composition <id>`) at the moments you edited, and read the frames before you reply. A passing check does not show how it looks.

## Key Rules

1. Every timed element needs `data-start` and a duration. `data-start` is what marks it as timed; `data-track-index` is an optional Studio display lane the render never reads
2. Give timed visual elements `class="clip"`. The framework keys visibility off `data-start`, not the class, but the shared `.clip` CSS is what gives a scene its full-frame box, and `lint` warns without it
3. Register one paused root timeline per composition on `window.__timelines`:
   ```js
   window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {};
   window.__timelines["composition-id"] = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
   ```
   Scene timelines manually added to this root must not be paused. A paused
   child does not advance when the root is seeked. The runtime activates
   registered composition siblings, not arbitrary nested scene timelines.
4. A video with sound keeps it on the `<video>` (`data-has-audio="true"`, no `muted`). Use a separate `<audio>` for music, voiceover, replacement audio, J/L cuts, or audio detached in Studio. Silent footage and b-roll: `muted`.
5. Sub-compositions use `data-composition-src="compositions/file.html"` to reference other HTML files
6. Only deterministic logic — no `Date.now()`, no `Math.random()`, no network fetches

The first-time inventory walkthrough is ready to review:

**[Watch the preview](http://localhost:3004/#project/inventory)**

The HyperFrames check passed with no errors. The example handover shows a disabled checkout because the seeded loan dates have passed. I haven’t rendered the MP4 yet.
